source: Stupple & Ball (2008) Belief-logic conflict resolution in syllogistic reasoning: inspection-time evidence for a parallel-process model
finding: Replicates the classic logic-by-belief interaction. Believable conclusions are accepted more. The belief effect is bigger on invalid than valid problems. A harder figure (BA-CB) raised belief bias.
numbers: N=48 undergraduates, 16 target syllogisms each. Percent accepted, figure AB-BC (believable/unbelievable): valid 76/72, invalid 71/36. Figure BA-CB: valid 88/60, invalid 61/25. Logic F(1,47)=47.32; belief F=34.42; logic x belief F=9.15, p=.004; belief x figure F=6.17, p=.017; logic x belief x figure F=5.40, p=.025. In the hard figure the logic x belief interaction vanished.
limits: One experiment, mouse-contingent display, definitional-truth contents. No logic x figure interaction (p=.10), so authors doubt the complexity manipulation fully worked. Author draft, not the copyedited version.
agent_relevance: On harder problems belief pulls on valid and invalid alike. Expect our model to lean on content more as problem difficulty rises; test at several difficulty levels.

source: Stupple & Ball (2008) Belief-logic conflict resolution in syllogistic reasoning: inspection-time evidence for a parallel-process model
finding: Time spent on premises depends on whether belief and logic conflict. Conflict problems (valid-unbelievable, invalid-believable) got longer premise inspection. This was predicted by parallel-process models, not by belief-first selective scrutiny.
numbers: Premise inspection: logic x belief F(1,47)=9.74, p=.003; logic main effect F=5.90, p=.02 (invalid longer); belief main effect F=0.38, p=.54 (null). Valid-unbelievable > valid-believable p=.027; invalid-believable > valid-believable p=.001; invalid-believable > invalid-unbelievable p=.12 (ns). Conclusion inspection: figure F=4.53 p=.039, logic F=12.70 p=.001, belief F=0.24 (null).
quote: the premises of conflict problems (valid-unbelievable and invalid-unbelievable ones) being inspected substantially longer than the premises of non-conflict problems
limits: Null belief effects may be low power (authors say so). Earlier work (Thompson et al. 2003) found people spent MORE time on believable conclusions, the opposite of selective scrutiny. The paper's wording lists valid-unbelievable and invalid-unbelievable as conflict in one sentence, which looks like a typo for invalid-believable.
agent_relevance: People appear to detect belief-logic conflict even when they answer wrongly. A cheap conflict signal (the believability judgment and the validity judgment disagree) could trigger extra checking, in line with G1 (doubt on a signal).

source: Stupple & Ball (2008) Belief-logic conflict resolution in syllogistic reasoning: inspection-time evidence for a parallel-process model
finding: Sorts belief-bias theories into three families with different predictions. Belief-first: selective scrutiny (Evans, Barston, Pollard 1983) and default-interventionist selective processing (Evans 2000, 2007). Reasoning-first (escape hatch): misinterpreted necessity and Quayle and Ball's metacognitive uncertainty theory. Parallel-process: Sloman's associative and rule-based systems running together.
numbers: Predictions listed: selective scrutiny expects longer inspection of unbelievable-conclusion problems at any complexity; selective processing expects more bias under speeded instructions (Evans and Curtis-Holmes 2005) and does not expect longer unbelievable inspection; reasoning-first expects faster valid responding and more bias on complex problems; parallel-process expects longer times on conflict problems.
limits: The three-way taxonomy is credited to Evans (personal communication). It describes theory families, not one agreed theory; the paper says all current theories gain some support.
agent_relevance: The families disagree on whether the model checks logic only when the belief is disliked. For our agent: do not assume a believable-looking answer gets lighter checking unless a signal says so; make S4 test every candidate the same way.

source: Stupple & Ball (2008) Belief-logic conflict resolution in syllogistic reasoning: inspection-time evidence for a parallel-process model
finding: Selective scrutiny was supported by Evans and Pollard (1990): a complexity manipulation changed discrimination of valid from invalid but not the size of the belief effect. Klauer, Musch and Naumer (2000) reread the same data: lower variance in complex groups implies the relative impact of belief was larger there.
numbers: No new numbers; reanalysis claim only (Klauer et al. 2000, p. 856). Selective processing model: default is accept believable and reject unbelievable; analytic stage builds one model and searches for a confirming model if the conclusion is believable and a falsifying model if unbelievable (Evans 2000, 2007; Evans, Handley and Harper 2001).
limits: Second-hand description of Evans and Pollard 1990 and Klauer et al. 2000 (neither opened). The complexity-by-belief result is unsettled.
agent_relevance: Search direction (confirm vs refute) depends on whether the answer matches belief. Our S4 should always include a refutation attempt, not only a confirming run.

source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning, as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Three experiments with controls for atmosphere, conversion and carry-over. They found a belief effect on both valid and invalid syllogisms, somewhat larger on invalid ones, and better sensitivity to validity when the conclusion was unbelievable. They also criticized Revlin et al. (1980) for a multiple-choice measure that counted two of four options as plausible, mostly valid items and no atmosphere control.
numbers: No cell percentages or N in the secondary text. Thesis: the interaction between belief and validity is the key result later models must explain.
limits: SECONDARY description only; the 1983 paper itself was paywalled and not opened. Memory and Cognition 11(3), 295-306 (bibliographic data from a search result).
agent_relevance: The founding design is a 2x2 (valid/invalid by believable/unbelievable) with matched structure. That is the exact test set we should build for S4 (content-swapped items).

source: Evans, Barston & Pollard (1983) as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Selective scrutiny: the reasoner first judges whether the conclusion is believable. If believable, accept without deduction. If unbelievable, reason logically and reject more often. Logic is driven by disbelief. Compared by the thesis to Lord, Ross and Lepper (1979) biased assimilation: people attack contradicting evidence harder than confirming evidence.
numbers: No numbers in this passage.
limits: Secondary text. Later work (Stupple and Ball 2008; Ball et al. 2006; Thompson et al. 2003) found inspection-time patterns that do not fit it.
agent_relevance: A model that scrutinizes only answers it dislikes will keep wrong believable answers. Guardrail G2/G3 (revise from real output, test on held-out items) addresses this: scrutiny must not depend on whether the answer feels right.

source: Markovits & Nantel (1989) and Evans & Pollard (1990), Newstead et al. (1992), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Misinterpreted necessity: when a conclusion is possible but not forced by the premises (indeterminate invalid syllogism), people feel unsure and fall back on belief. Markovits and Nantel used a production task and found more belief bias on invalid items. Later versions added that uncertainty also arises on complex valid and determinately invalid items.
numbers: No numbers given in the secondary text. Dube et al. (2010) call it an escape-hatch mechanism when deductive reasoning is inconclusive.
limits: Secondary text. The original model was silent on bias for valid and determinate-invalid items; the Evans and Pollard / Newstead caveat patched this.
agent_relevance: Belief takes over when the logic returns 'cannot tell'. Our agent should treat an inconclusive internal check as a trigger to look for a decisive test, not to fall back on plausibility.

source: Oakhill, Johnson-Laird & Garnham (1989) and Newstead et al. (1992), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Mental models account: build a model of the premises (comprehension), form or compare a conclusion (description), then try to build counter-model(s) (validation). Real deduction happens only at validation. A believable conclusion that fits the first model is accepted without validation; an unbelievable one triggers a search for alternative models. This differs from selective scrutiny, where plausibility is checked first.
numbers: Oakhill et al. 1989 compared one-model valid, indeterminate and multiple-model valid items with plausible or implausible content. One-model and indeterminate items showed the belief effect; multiple-model valid items gave inconclusive results (too many models to juggle). Evans et al. 1983 did find a belief effect on multiple-model problems, so the two sets disagree.
limits: Secondary text; numbers not given. The disagreement on multiple-model problems is unresolved in the sources opened.
agent_relevance: Search for counter-examples fails when there are too many to hold at once. The agent should externalize counter-example search (code or enumeration) for multi-premise problems instead of relying on in-head models.

source: Newstead, Pollard, Evans & Allen (1992) The source of belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning, as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Belief bias was equal on determinately invalid and valid items, which fits misinterpreted necessity and not selective scrutiny. Contrasting misinterpreted necessity with mental models on single-model items favoured mental models. Later experiments: the interaction returns with multiple-model items, and instructions stressing a logical strategy reduced bias.
numbers: Five experiments (abstract seen in a search result: Experiments 1 and 2 removed the interaction when only determinate syllogisms were used; Experiment 3 favoured mental models; Experiments 4 and 5 followed up). No cell data seen.
limits: Secondary description; the 1992 paper (Cognition 45, 257-284) was paywalled.
agent_relevance: Removing indeterminate items removed the interaction, so a large part of the effect comes from ambiguous items. When we build test sets, keep determinate and indeterminate items separate.

source: Polk & Newell (1995) verbal reasoning theory and Thompson et al. (2003), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Verbal reasoning theory is a computational model that solves syllogisms by linguistic term manipulation. It reproduced human belief bias by adding annotations for plausible and implausible statements: when an implausible conclusion was generated the model re-encoded the premises, and if that failed it chose at random between 'not valid' and a belief-based conclusion. Thompson et al. (2003) revised it: search for one integrating model until a deadline, with a longer deadline for believable content.
numbers: Thompson et al. 2003: people spent MORE time on believable than unbelievable conclusions; believable invalid items were slow, believable valid items fast; the number of diagrams drawn did not differ across conditions.
limits: Secondary text. The random-choice fallback is a simulation detail of Polk and Newell, not a human measurement.
agent_relevance: A small program already reproduces the bias with a rule 'if reasoning fails, guess toward belief'. The same failure rule is a risk for an LLM: if its check fails, it may guess toward the plausible answer. G6 (best attempt, no abstention) should be paired with a flag when the final answer came from a failed check.

source: Klauer, Musch & Naumer (2000) On belief bias in syllogistic reasoning (Psychological Review 107, 852-884), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Multinomial processing tree (MPT) model. Reasoning first succeeds with a probability that depends on structure and belief. If it fails (uncertainty), a response stage guesses, using extra-logical cues: belief, atmosphere, and the believed base rate of valid items. Belief also sets the search goal: confirming tests for believable conclusions and falsifying tests for unbelievable ones. Four trees, one per cell of the 2x2.
numbers: 8 experiments (lab and web). The base-rate cue (told many, some or few arguments are valid) interacted with belief only in the response stage. Logic-trained participants reasoned to a result more often and guessed less, but when guessing were no more or less belief-driven than novices. Guess-valid probability treated as a product of the expected validity rate and conclusion plausibility.
limits: Secondary text; paper itself not opened. Garnham and Oakhill (2005) dispute the mapping of the mental-models account onto this model and say it explains Experiments 1-4 and 5-8.
agent_relevance: The cleanest formal account: belief matters most in the guess stage. For the agent this suggests measuring a guess-rate and a belief-on-guess rate separately, and manipulating the told base rate of valid items in tests.

source: Garnham & Oakhill (2005) Accounting for belief bias in a mental model framework: comment on Klauer, Musch, and Naumer (2000)
finding: A defense of the mental-models account against the multinomial model. They argue it does not map onto Klauer et al.'s model, that it explains Klauer's Experiments 1-4, and that the Experiments 5-8 data in support of Klauer's own model are also explained by it.
numbers: No new data (PubMed abstract of Psychological Review 112(2), 509-518).
limits: Abstract only. Klauer and colleagues replied (title 'Accounting for belief bias in a mental model framework? No problem!'); reply not opened.
agent_relevance: Formal models here are hard to separate with accuracy data alone. Treat any single mechanism story about why the LLM is biased as unproven; rely on measured effects.

source: Dube, Rotello & Heit (2010) Assessing the belief bias effect with ROCs: it's a response bias effect (Psychological Review 117, 831-863)
finding: The standard 'contrast of contrasts' belief-bias measure assumes linear ROCs (a threshold model). In 3 experiments with confidence ratings (and a base-rate manipulation in one), the empirical ROCs were curved. Under a signal-detection model the belief effect appears as a response-bias shift, not an accuracy effect. They call the accuracy effect a Type I error and favour graded argument-strength accounts such as Chater and Oaksford's probability heuristics model.
numbers: 3 experiments; no cell values in the abstract.
quote: belief bias effect is simply a response bias effect
limits: Abstract only. Contested: Klauer and Kellen (2011) argue binary-response ROCs are linear and that confidence-rating ROCs can create curvature. Trippas et al. (2013) found believability affects accuracy on complex items.
agent_relevance: Key warning for our measurement: do not read a drop in accuracy on unbelievable valid items as proof of worse reasoning; it may be a changed willingness to say 'valid'. Collect a confidence or a graded score and report both sensitivity and bias.

source: Dube, Rotello & Heit (2011) The belief bias effect is aptly named: a reply to Klauer and Kellen (2011)
finding: Reply with new data and model-based analyses. They say the logic-by-belief interaction is an artefact of using hit rate minus false-alarm rate, that Klauer and Kellen's objections were speculation about the confidence-rating method, and that Klauer and Kellen's own new modelling supports Dube et al.
numbers: No numbers in abstract.
limits: Abstract only; self-interested reply in an ongoing dispute.
agent_relevance: The field has not settled whether belief changes accuracy or only the yes-threshold. Our agent design should not depend on either answer being settled.

source: Klauer & Kellen (2011) Assessing the belief bias effect with ROCs: reply to Dube, Rotello, and Heit (2010) (Psychological Review 118, 164-173)
finding: Reanalysis of Dube et al.'s data and of old data. ROCs are linear for binary valid/invalid responses (the bulk of the field). Klauer et al.'s model fits old data significantly better than Dube's SDT model and Dube's own data somewhat better. Dube's data are consistent with misinterpreted necessity, while the SDT model does not fit them. Belief bias is more than a response bias effect.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Singmann and Kellen (2014) later show SDT models of this design are not identifiable without extra assumptions.
agent_relevance: A second reason to avoid a single-metric claim. We will report accuracy by cell (VB, VU, IB, IU) in addition to any summary index.

source: Heit & Rotello (2014) Traditional difference-score analyses of reasoning are flawed (Cognition 131, 75-91)
finding: Simulations show the three traditional indices (logic, belief, interaction) can lead to wrong conclusions. Two new experiments on instructional manipulations gave ROCs that violate assumptions of those indices. SDT analyses implied belief bias and instruction effects are mostly response bias. Re-analysis of conditional reasoning data also gave non-linear ROCs.
numbers: Two new experiments; numbers not in abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Same research group as Dube et al., so not independent of that dispute.
agent_relevance: Instruction changes (like 'think logically') may move the threshold for saying valid rather than improving discrimination. When we test instruction prompts we must separate these two effects.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2013) The SDT model of belief bias: complexity, time, and cognitive ability mediate the effects of believability (JEP:LMC 39, 1393-1402)
finding: Counter-evidence to a pure response-bias view. ROC analysis showed believability affected accuracy for complex but not for simple syllogisms (Exp 1). Under time pressure and in people with low cognitive capacity the accuracy effect of believability disappeared (Exp 2). Beliefs influence more than response bias when conditions allow certain reasoning strategies.
numbers: Numbers not in the abstract (later cited by Trippas et al. 2014 as: time pressure reduced sensitivity and the belief-accuracy effect among higher-ability participants; higher-ability people were more influenced by belief in the reasoning stage, lower-ability mainly showed response bias).
limits: Abstract plus a later summary. Result depends on the ability split and on the SDT identifiability assumptions criticized by Singmann and Kellen (2014).
agent_relevance: Belief's effect on accuracy needs spare capacity: able reasoners use it as motivated reasoning (try harder on unbelievable items). For our agent, spare budget should be spent preferentially where the answer conflicts with a prior.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2014) Fluency and belief bias in deductive reasoning: new indices for old effects (Frontiers in Psychology 5:631)
finding: Defines the traditional indices and SDT replacements. Traditional: logic = VB+VU-IB-IU; belief = VB+IB-VU-IU; interaction = VU+IB-VB-IU (rates of 'valid' responses). SDT: da = sqrt(2/(1+s^2)) [z(H) - s z(F)], ca similarly; SDT logic index = da, SDT belief index = ca(unbelievable) - ca(believable), SDT interaction index = da(unbelievable) - da(believable). s (the ROC slope) is estimated from 3-point confidence ratings.
numbers: Cites simulations (Heit and Rotello 2014) showing traditional indices inflate Type I error. Recommends collecting confidence on every judgment.
limits: Methods article; it notes that full model fitting can need too many parameters, so the indices are a shortcut. Equal-variance d' is not recommended because variance of valid and invalid distributions often differs.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready recipe for our own measurement harness: confidence-coded validity judgments from the model, then da and ca by believability cell.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2014) Fluency and belief bias in deductive reasoning (Frontiers in Psychology 5:631)
finding: Disfluent text (hard to read) was predicted to improve reasoning but lowered it. Disfluency did not change belief-based response bias. Cognitive ability raised accuracy and lowered response bias (replicating earlier work). Disfluency removed the usual link between ability and the belief-accuracy effect.
numbers: N=76 undergraduates (38 per condition), 64 syllogisms, 3-level confidence. All participants: above chance t(75)=8.41, standard belief bias t(75)=6.72, belief affected accuracy t(75)=2.81 p=.006. Accuracy: fluent da=0.92 (Az=74%), disfluent da=0.51 (Az=64%), F(1,74)=6.22, p=.015, eta-squared=.078, BF=3.30. Fluency effect on SDT belief index F<1, p=.36, BF=0.34. Higher-ability da 1.06 vs lower 0.42.
limits: Between-subject, undergraduates, one disfluency manipulation, Raven short form (max 12). Bayes factor for the main effect is only moderate.
agent_relevance: Making the input harder to read lowered reasoning accuracy. A noisy or long messy prompt could do the same to an LLM, so S1 (restating the problem cleanly) has a measurable reason to exist.

source: Singmann & Kellen (2014) Concerns with the SDT approach to causal conditional reasoning: a comment on Trippas et al. (2014) (Frontiers in Psychology 5:402)
finding: A 2x2 SDT design with separate criteria for believable and unbelievable items is unidentifiable: differences in evidence-distribution means trade off with differences in response criteria. Fixing the invalid-believable mean to 0 forces a pure criterion-shift reading. Criterion shifts from trial to trial are also implausible given other work.
numbers: Their refit: SDT fits the linear aggregate ROCs better (VB/IB G2(3)=7.95, p=.05; VU/IU G2(3)=10.63, p=.01) than the curvilinear ROCs.
limits: Concerns causal-conditional data; applies by argument to syllogisms too. Technical; read as a methods warning, not a result about people.
agent_relevance: Do not over-trust any single decomposition of bias vs sensitivity. Prefer raw per-cell accuracy plus a held-out check.

source: Trippas, Verde, Handley, Roser, McNair & Evans (2014) Modeling causal conditional reasoning data using SDT: caveats and new insights (Frontiers in Psychology 5:217)
finding: Applies SDT to causal conditionals with believable and unbelievable contents. Reported that believability changed response bias without changing reasoning quality, and that the ROCs were curvilinear, as SDT predicts.
numbers: Only the opening column was read (no sample sizes). Authors list Dube et al. 2011 and Trippas et al. 2013 as curvilinear and Klauer and Kellen 2011 as the dissent.
limits: Opinion article, partially read. Contested by Singmann and Kellen (2014).
agent_relevance: Belief effects may be similar across syllogisms and conditionals; so content-swap tests should include if-then problems.

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias (Memory & Cognition)
finding: Participants judged either validity or believability of the same conclusion. Under a default-interventionist model, belief answers are faster and belief should interfere with logic but not the reverse. Data showed interference depends on how complex the logical structure is: modus ponens validity interfered with belief judgments more; moderate complexity gave symmetric interference; the hardest syllogisms gave belief interfering more with logic judgments.
numbers: Exp 1: N=45, 2x2x2 within, 64 arguments (modus ponens and modus tollens). Exp 2: N=84 (Saskatchewan), simple vs complex syllogisms.
limits: Author list taken from memory of the journal record; the PMC page text shows title and abstract. Response times analysed after boxplot outlier removal.
agent_relevance: Fast logic can beat belief on easy problems. So belief bias is not 'System 1 always wins'; it grows with logical difficulty. Spend compute by difficulty (G12).

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief
finding: Exp 2 accuracy: conflict items were harder than no-conflict. On the complex syllogisms with logic instructions, accuracy on conflict items fell to chance (.50). Belief instructions were far easier than logic instructions on complex problems.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=84 minus 2 excluded): conflict M=.68 vs no-conflict .83, OR=1.58; complex .71 vs simple .80. Simple: belief-instruction conflict .73 / no-conflict .87; logic .72 / .90. Complex: belief .76 / .85; logic .50 / .71. Complex problems, conflict effect under logic instructions diff=.21 vs belief diff=.09, interaction chi2(1)=4.86, p=.03, OR=1.14.
quote: performance for conflict items under logic instructions was at chance levels
limits: Within-subject undergraduate samples; one syllogism set. Complexity defined by mental-model count and by a probability-heuristics argument.
agent_relevance: With hard multi-model syllogisms the conflict case is at chance, so any LLM test set needs hard items to show the bias.

source: Evans & Curtis-Holmes (2005) Rapid responding increases belief bias, as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: A response time limit raised belief bias and lowered logical accuracy. The harm fell mostly on incongruent (conflict) items; on congruent items free-time and limited-time accuracy differed little. Interpreted as dual-process support: the time limit stops the analytic search for alternative models.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary text. The exact deadline is reported inconsistently across the sources I saw: 10 seconds in a bibliographic abstract from a search result (not opened), and 2 seconds in a Wikipedia summary.
limits: Secondary description; Thinking & Reasoning 11(4), 382-389 not opened (paywalled). Exact N and rates unavailable here.
agent_relevance: A short reasoning budget should raise belief-driven errors on conflict items more than on agreeing items. Test: vary token cap and measure the gap between VB and VU accuracy.

source: Reverberi, Rusconi, Paulesu & Cherubini (2009) as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Under a limit under 20 seconds, atmosphere (a structural heuristic) was the main surface cue and belief was a secondary cue mostly affecting conflict items. The structural heuristic disappeared with more time, while belief bias remained under both limited and unlimited time.
numbers: Limit stated as under 20 s; no further numbers.
limits: Secondary description only. The paper itself was not read.
agent_relevance: Beliefs are the persistent bias, while structural shortcuts fade with more thinking time. Longer reasoning will not by itself remove content effects.

source: Evans, Newstead, Allen & Pollard (1994) as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Instructions telling people to accept only conclusions that must be true did NOT remove belief bias. A broader instruction (explaining that 'some' means at least one and possibly all, and to rely only on the given information) reduced acceptance of invalid-believable conclusions, but did not eliminate the bias.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary text.
limits: Secondary description. This conflicts with SUBFIELDS.md, which says logical-necessity instructions lower belief bias, and partly with Newstead et al. (1992), who report that logic-stressing instructions attenuate it. The thesis text and Macchi et al. disagree on how effective 'necessity' wording is.
agent_relevance: A short 'think logically' instruction may do little; a specific instruction that fixes how quantifiers and 'given information only' are to be read may do more. Test both and report separately.

source: Macchi, Poli, Caravona, Vezzoli, Franchella & Bagassi, How to get rid of the belief bias: boosting analytical thinking via pragmatics (Europe's Journal of Psychology; year approx.)
finding: With the plain question 'Does the conclusion follow from the premises?' almost everyone accepted an invalid-believable syllogism, even people trained in logic.
numbers: Exp 1: N=130 (50 untrained, 80 logic-trained), one valid-believable (All animals are mortal...) and one invalid-believable item (All roses are flowers). Valid-believable correct: 94% untrained, 96% trained. Invalid-believable correct: 4% untrained, 10% trained (no group difference, chi2=1.56, p=.31; BF 8.52 for no difference).
limits: Two items only per person; paper-and-pencil; year of publication inferred (JASP 2018 cited), not read from the page.
agent_relevance: Logic training did not protect against bias when the instruction did not signal logic. Prompt wording may matter more than the model's capacity to do logic.

source: Macchi et al., How to get rid of the belief bias: boosting analytical thinking via pragmatics
finding: Changing one phrase in the instruction produced a large gain on the same invalid-believable item. 'Does the conclusion necessarily follow?' worked even for untrained people.
numbers: Exp 2: N=162 (101 untrained, 61 trained). Correct on invalid-believable: 'necessarily' wording 66% untrained, 77% trained (no group difference, p=.45); 'criteria of logic' wording 41% untrained, 67% trained (p=.03). Control (Exp 1) 4% and 10%. Control vs 'necessarily': chi2=42.24 (untrained), 47.91 (trained), p<.001.
quote: Does the conclusion necessarily follow from the given premises?
limits: Single item, between-subject, control group from a previous experiment (not randomized in the same session). Authors say earlier attempts to reduce bias often failed or did not replicate. A large effect on one item may not generalize.
agent_relevance: Strong lead for our instruction tests: ask 'does it necessarily follow' rather than 'is this correct'. Needs replication across many items and with a model, not just people (conflicts with the 1994 finding above).

source: Stupple, Ball, Evans & Kamal-Smith (2011), as described in Macchi et al.
finding: Low-performing participants answered more quickly than high-performing ones. All groups answered more quickly on no-conflict than conflict problems, hinting that even poor reasoners notice the conflict. Macchi et al. argue the real gap is understanding what the task asks.
numbers: Participants were split into 3 groups by performance on belief-biased syllogisms; no numbers in the secondary text.
limits: Secondary description. Authors interpret slower = more analytic; Macchi et al. say that does not show greater logical ability.
agent_relevance: Detecting conflict is common and cheap, so a conflict flag between the plausible answer and a derived answer is a usable trigger (G1).

source: De Neys & Franssens (2009) Belief inhibition during thinking, as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: People who solved conflict syllogisms correctly were slower at recognising words related to the belief content afterwards, suggesting they had to inhibit the belief. Failures look like inhibition started but not finished.
numbers: Best conflict solvers averaged 93% correct; worst solved 0% (group comparison in the thesis). Detection of neutral words unaffected.
limits: Secondary description; lexical-decision method; N not given.
agent_relevance: Belief is active even when the answer is correct, so a plausible competitor is always present. A check against the plausible competitor is the right target for S4.

source: Ball, Phillips, Wade & Quayle (2006) Effects of belief and logic on syllogistic reasoning: eye-movement evidence for selective processing models (Experimental Psychology 53, 77-86)
finding: Eye-tracking inspection times supported selective-processing theories: believability biases model construction, not the search for falsifying models and not a late uncertain response stage. Per the thesis, people looked at premises for about 4 seconds before the conclusion, then longer at premises after the conclusion in incongruent problems.
numbers: No cell values in abstract. Thesis summary: no valid/invalid time difference (no support for selective scrutiny); post-conclusion premise inspection longer for believable than unbelievable (against mental models).
limits: Abstract plus second-hand summary. Stupple and Ball (2008) note a confound in this study: validity was tied to premise configuration.
agent_relevance: Reasoners seem to use the conclusion as the anchor and re-read the premises backwards. Hide the conclusion until the premises are restated (S1/S2), or treat it as a hypothesis, so the answer does not anchor the reading.

source: Stupple & Ball (2007), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: With neutral contents, premise inspection followed the figure: BA-CB premises were inspected much longer than AB-BC and needed a revisit of Premise 1. This supports forward (premises-first) reasoning, unlike the backward pattern found with belief-laden conclusions in Ball et al. 2006.
numbers: No numbers in secondary text.
limits: Secondary description. The authors suggest forward reasoning may be used more for neutral problems and backward reasoning when the conclusion is belief-relevant.
agent_relevance: Belief-laden conclusions may change reading order. Restate the problem with neutral labels (S1/S2) and compare to the original wording as a content-swap test.

source: Wikipedia, Belief bias (page fetched; secondary, summarised by a small model during fetch)
finding: Reports the classic percentages as: believable conclusions accepted 80% vs unbelievable 33%; valid 73% vs invalid 41%. The page also lists Evans and Curtis-Holmes (2005), Goel and Vartanian (2011; N=34, negative emotional content reduced belief bias and slowed responses), Markovits and Nantel (1989), Torrens (2010), Dube et al. (2010).
numbers: 80% vs 33% (believable vs unbelievable); 73% vs 41% (valid vs invalid); the fetch also returned 89% (believable-valid) and 56% (unbelievable-invalid), which look inconsistent with the other figures.
limits: UNVERIFIED against the 1983 paper. I could not find the original table of cell percentages in any source I opened. Do not use these as a benchmark until checked. The text I saw does not describe selective scrutiny or misinterpreted necessity.
agent_relevance: Treat 80/33 as a rough target for human data only. We measure our own cells.

source: Gilinsky & Judd (1994) and De Neys & Van Gelder (2009), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: Older adults show more belief bias on neutral content and have particular trouble with 3-model syllogisms; working memory and vocabulary decline independently predicted low accuracy. De Neys and Van Gelder: children and older adults did worse than young adults on conflict items, a pattern linked to weak belief inhibition (a curved trend across the lifespan).
numbers: No numbers in secondary text.
limits: Secondary description. Related individual-difference work: Sa, West and Stanovich (1999) found higher SAT score, more open-minded thinking and better decontextualization go with less belief-based responding (per Macchi et al.).
agent_relevance: Capacity (working memory, inhibition) predicts resistance. Smaller models are the likelier victims; test by model size.

source: Janis & Frick (1943), Morgan & Morton (1944), Henle (1962) and Revlin et al. (1980), as described in Hilscher (2014) Attenuating belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (PhD thesis, Univ. Toronto; literature review chapters, used as a secondary source)
finding: History: Janis and Frick (1943) first labelled the belief bias effect; critics said atmosphere could explain it. Morgan and Morton (1944) pitted atmosphere against belief and found belief won more often. Henle (1962) argued many errors come from interpreting premises differently, not from bad logic. Revlin et al. (1980) argued errors are atmosphere or conversion effects, and were criticized by Evans et al. 1983.
numbers: No numbers in the secondary text.
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Interpretation of the task (what a premise means, what 'valid' means) is a recurring confound. S1 should fix the reading of quantifiers before reasoning.

source: Newstead, Pollard, Evans & Allen (1992) The source of belief bias effects in syllogistic reasoning (abstract seen in a search result)
finding: Abstract (as relayed by a search summary) says Experiments 1 and 2 found the interaction disappears with determinate syllogisms only, supporting misinterpreted necessity; Experiment 3 favoured mental models; Experiments 4 and 5 supported mental models too. Conclusion: people build a mental model and, if a believable conclusion fits the first model, fail to build alternatives.
numbers: Cognition 45(3), 257-284. No data seen.
limits: Not opened; reported through a web-search summary and a thesis.
agent_relevance: See a09.

source: Evans & Curtis-Holmes (2005) Rapid responding increases belief bias (abstract seen in a search result)
finding: Bibliographic abstract (via search) says belief bias in syllogisms was compared under standard presentation and a time limit; with the limit belief bias rose and logical decisions fell, read as support for dual-process theory.
numbers: Deadline reported as 10 seconds in that abstract; conflicts with the 2-second figure seen on Wikipedia. Not resolved.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: See a24 for the time-limit prediction.
